Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports business payments to suppliers, vendors, contractors, and other businesses for commercial transactions, procurement, and supply chain payments.
Comments: B2B payments functionality is supported via the banking and interoperable payment ecosystem (GIMACPAY includes transfer services for participants such as banks, payment institutions, and public treasuries), but public evidence tying this explicitly to a B2B use case in Cameroon is limited, so scored conservatively.
revision_notes: Fetched and read the AfricaNenda SIIPS 2023 CEMAC case study on GIMACPAY. Its 'Use Cases & Target Market' table explicitly lists 'Inventory and Business Services (B2B)' alongside P2P, B2P, P2B, cross-border, P2G and G2P as a recognised use case supported by the system, in addition to the prose confirming a broad range of use cases. This is a clear, authoritative, fetched source directly contradicting the conservative 'No' score, so the code is raised to 2 (Yes).
revised_comments: GIMACPAY, the CEMAC region's interoperable instant payment system operating in Cameroon under Bank of Central African States (BEAC) oversight, supports business-to-business payments as one of its recognised use cases, alongside person-to-person transfers, merchant payments, cross-border transfers, salary disbursements and government payments, per AfricaNenda's State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems 2023 case study on GIMACPAY.

revision_notes: Fetched and read both original cited sources plus the AfricaNenda SIIPS 2023 CEMAC case study, whose use-case table lists 'Transfers and Remittances (P2P)' as a core GIMACPAY use case. Mobile money (MTN Mobile Money, Orange Money) further confirms widespread P2P transfer availability. Score of 2 (Yes) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Person-to-person transfers are a core, established use case of GIMACPAY, the CEMAC region's interoperable instant payment system, and are also widely available through mobile money services such as MTN Mobile Money and Orange Money. AfricaNenda's SIIPS 2023 case study lists transfers and remittances (P2P) among GIMACPAY's recognised use cases.

Definition: Whether and how the central bank participates in payment system governance beyond its regulatory oversight role, including board representation, operational management, technical standard-setting, or direct system operation.
Comments: BEAC directly operates/oversees core payment infrastructure and settlement (SYGMA RTGS; payment systems oversight) and is the dominant owner/settlement agent for GIMACPAY governance, indicating strong central-bank governance.
revision_notes: Fetched and read the AfricaNenda SIIPS 2023 CEMAC case study in full. Its governance model table distinguishes the 'Payment System Settlement Agent' (BEAC) from the 'System Manager', 'System Operator' and 'Technical System and Network Operator' (all GIMAC). BEAC owns 99.2% of GIMAC and mandated its creation via a 2018 interoperability directive, giving it a dominant governance and ownership role, but the report explicitly assigns day-to-day system governance and technical operation to GIMAC as a distinct entity rather than to BEAC directly. This is a judgement call between 'Board Representation' (4) and 'Direct Operation' (5); the source evidence better supports majority ownership plus settlement/oversight (4) than literal direct operation of the system by the central bank, so the code is revised down from 5 to 4. Flagged for human review given the closeness of the call.
revised_comments: The Bank of Central African States (BEAC) plays a dominant governance role in GIMACPAY, the CEMAC region's instant payment system: it owns 99.2% of GIMAC, the entity established to run the scheme, mandated the system's creation through a 2018 interoperability directive, and acts as settlement agent via its SYGMA real-time gross settlement platform. Day-to-day system governance and technical operation are carried out by GIMAC as the designated operator, so the central bank's involvement is best characterised as majority ownership with settlement and oversight functions rather than direct operation of the payment system itself.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: General privacy/data protection exists via Cameroon’s Law No. 2010/012 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (general protections around data/security), but no clear payments-specific data privacy law was evidenced in the materials reviewed.
revision_notes: The originally cited 2010 cybersecurity law and 2020 lexafrica overview are now superseded: Cameroon enacted a dedicated, comprehensive Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024 on personal data protection, confirmed by fetching the African Law & Business analysis and the official gazette text. The Act is GDPR-aligned (portability, impact assessments, records of processing, cross-border transfer rules) and creates a dedicated Personal Data Protection Authority, and explicitly classifies banking transaction data as 'sensitive data' requiring enhanced protection. This is still a general data protection framework rather than payment-sector-specific legislation, so the code (2 = General Data Protection Legislation) is unchanged, but the evidentiary basis and year are substantially updated.
revised_comments: Cameroon enacted comprehensive personal data protection legislation, Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024, establishing a dedicated Personal Data Protection Authority and GDPR-aligned obligations including data portability rights, data protection impact assessments, records-of-processing requirements and cross-border transfer conditions. The Act classifies banking transaction data as a category of sensitive personal data attracting enhanced protection, though it remains a general data protection framework rather than legislation specific to payment services. Compliance is required by 23 June 2026.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: Pro-poor/inclusion governance exists but is partial: Cameroon’s National Strategy for Inclusive Finance (SNFI 2023–2027) targets vulnerable groups (rural populations, women, youth, MSMEs), and the BEAC-led CNEF performs consumer protection/mediation functions, but there is limited evidence of a comprehensive, enforceable pro-poor governance framework specific to instant payments scheme governance.
revision_notes: The minfi.gov.cm source could not be fetched (crawl timeout), but its substance is corroborated by the UNCDF Policy Accelerator article, which was fetched and read: it confirms Cameroon's National Inclusive Finance Strategy (SNFI), published February 2023, targets vulnerable groups (rural populations, women, youth, MSMEs), and that the BEAC-led National Economic and Financial Committee (CNEF) performs consumer protection and dispute-resolution functions. No evidence found of a comprehensive, enforceable pro-poor governance mandate written into GIMACPAY's own scheme governance documents specifically, so the 'Partial' score (2) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Cameroon's National Inclusive Finance Strategy (SNFI), published in February 2023, targets vulnerable populations including rural communities, women, youth and MSMEs, and the Bank of Central African States (BEAC)-led National Economic and Financial Committee (CNEF) provides consumer protection and complaint-resolution functions for financial services users, including digital payments. These mechanisms provide partial coverage of pro-poor governance principles but fall short of a comprehensive, enforceable inclusion mandate embedded directly within the instant payment system's own governance structure.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing an instant/real-time payment system (IPS/RTP) that enables digital payments with near-instant settlement (typically within seconds), available 24/7/365. This includes both bank-led and mobile money interoperability systems.
Comments: GIMACPAY (GIMAC interoperable instant payments ecosystem under BEAC oversight) has been live since July 2020 and provides real-time clearing for payments across CEMAC including Cameroon, with settlement via BEAC’s SYGMA RTGS, meeting “fully deployed” digital payments infrastructure criteria.
revision_notes: Fetched and read the SIIPS 2023 CEMAC case study plus AfricaNenda's SIIPS 2024/2025 material and the GIMAC website, confirming GIMACPAY has remained continuously live and operational since its July 2020 launch, now with over 90 participants (commercial banks, MMOs, MFIs, a public treasury and a post office) and cumulative transaction value exceeding FCFA 600 billion by 2025. This is a strong, current, multi-source evidence base supporting the maximum code (5 = Fully deployed nationwide), so the score is confirmed unchanged. As this is a top-of-scale (maximum) score, it is flagged for human review per protocol even though the evidence is authoritative and current.
revised_comments: GIMACPAY, the interoperable instant payment system covering Cameroon and the wider CEMAC region (Central African Republic, Chad, Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon), has operated continuously since its official launch in July 2020 under the oversight of the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), with settlement via BEAC's SYGMA real-time gross settlement platform. AfricaNenda's State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems reports confirm the system remains fully operational through 2025, with over 90 participants including commercial banks, mobile money operators, microfinance institutions, a public treasury and a post office, and cumulative transaction values exceeding FCFA 600 billion.
